text: What is the primary goal of Continuous Integration (CI) in DevOps pipelines?

options.A: Automatically building and testing code changes merged into a shared repository
options.B: Deploying the production server code to multiple clouds
options.C: Writing software documentation automatically using code parsers
options.D: Monitoring server CPU temperatures in real-time

explanation: CI focuses on automatically compiling, building, and running tests on new commits to catch bugs early in development.

text: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

options.A: Delivery requires manual approval to deploy to production; Deployment pushes code changes to production automatically
options.B: Deployment is for Docker; Delivery is only for legacy virtual machines
options.C: Continuous Delivery is slower because it builds code on local servers
options.D: There is no difference in modern DevOps automation terminology

explanation: Continuous Delivery prepares the build for release (allowing manual gates). Continuous Deployment automates the entire release directly to production.

text: Which pipeline element triggers a build automatically whenever a developer pushes a commit to the main branch?

options.A: Webhook / Trigger
options.B: Cron Schedule
options.C: Artifact repository link
options.D: Docker agent controller

explanation: Webhooks link Git hosts to CI servers, sending a webhook notification that triggers builds upon code pushes.

text: What is a 'build artifact' in CI/CD terms?

options.A: The compiled, ready-to-deploy output package of a build pipeline (e.g. zip, jar, docker image)
options.B: A piece of legacy code that is no longer used by the application
options.C: An error log indicating that the unit tests failed
options.D: The configuration file defining database credentials

explanation: Artifacts are the compiled, packaged output files generated during build steps, saved for testing or production deployment.

text: Which git command is used to record changes to the local repository history?

options.A: git commit
options.B: git add
options.C: git push
options.D: git clone

explanation: git commit saves your staged snapshots to the local commit history. git add stages them first; git push uploads them to remote.

text: What does 'git merge --no-ff' do?

options.A: Forces Git to create a merge commit even if a fast-forward merge is possible
options.B: Disables merge conflict detection during branch merges
options.C: Merges changes directly into the remote repository without committing locally
options.D: Cancels the merge operation and resets the working tree

explanation: The --no-ff (no fast-forward) flag creates a merge commit, preserving the historical existence of the feature branch.

text: What is 'git rebase' used for?

options.A: Applying commits from one branch on top of another to maintain a linear history
options.B: Reverting all committed changes back to the origin state
options.C: Deleting history logs to reduce the size of the repository folder
options.D: Merging multiple separate repositories into a monorepo structure

explanation: Rebase rewrites commits by moving the branch starting point (base) to a new commit, creating a clean linear path.

text: What is the primary difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?

options.A: An image is a read-only template; a container is a running, writable instance of that image
options.B: Images are hosted in the cloud; containers only run on local machines
options.C: Containers are compiled; images are written in HTML
options.D: There is no difference; they are interchangeable terms

explanation: An image contains the filesystem and configurations. A container is the isolated execution environment instantiated from that image.

text: In a Dockerfile, which instruction specifies the command that runs by default when the container starts?

options.A: CMD
options.B: RUN
options.C: FROM
options.D: COPY

explanation: CMD sets the default executable command for the container. RUN executes commands during the image build phase.

text: Why are multi-stage builds recommended in Dockerfile configurations?

options.A: They reduce the final container image size by stripping out build-time dependencies
options.B: They allow the container to run on both Linux and Windows concurrently
options.C: They double the speed of container startups in cloud clusters
options.D: They automatically encrypt the container storage filesystem

explanation: Multi-stage builds let you compile binaries in early stages, copying only the output binary to the final stage, excluding SDKs/source code.

text: What is the primary role of Kubernetes in DevOps environments?

options.A: To automate the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications
options.B: To write code files using terminal text editors
options.C: To compile TypeScript code to JavaScript
options.D: To monitor network bandwidth speeds at the office router

explanation: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform that coordinates cluster nodes and manages application lifecycles.

text: What is the smallest deployable unit of compute in a Kubernetes cluster?

options.A: Pod
options.B: Container
options.C: Service
options.D: Node

explanation: A Pod represents a single instance of a running process in your cluster, hosting one or more tightly coupled containers.

text: Which Kubernetes resource exposes a set of pods as a network service with a stable IP and DNS name?

options.A: Service
options.B: Deployment
options.C: ConfigMap
options.D: ReplicaSet

explanation: Kubernetes Services handle internal and external load balancing, keeping routing endpoints stable even as pods are recreated.

text: What is the function of the Kubernetes 'kubelet' agent?

options.A: It runs on each node to ensure containers are running in their assigned pods
options.B: It coordinates the scheduling of pods across the master node
options.C: It stores the configuration data and state of the cluster (etcd)
options.D: It serves the API endpoints to external CLI clients

explanation: The kubelet is the node agent that communicates with the control plane, monitoring container lifecycles on the host.

text: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?

options.A: Managing and provisioning infrastructure using machine-readable definition files
options.B: Writing code comments that explain server layouts
options.C: Storing database passwords inside the application code repository
options.D: Hosting virtual machines inside on-premises datacenters

explanation: IaC allows teams to configure networks, servers, and storage declaratively in code, automating environment creation.

text: Which command initializes a new or existing Terraform working directory by downloading provider plugins?

options.A: terraform init
options.B: terraform plan
options.C: terraform apply
options.D: terraform workspace

explanation: terraform init scans code files, configures backend state tracking, and downloads required cloud provider binaries.

text: What is the purpose of the 'terraform.tfstate' file?

options.A: It maps real-world resources to your configuration files to track state
options.B: It contains the temporary variables used during plans
options.C: It acts as a backup copy of the cloud provider account credentials
options.D: It compiles the Terraform code to binary machine code

explanation: The tfstate file records metadata and actual resource IDs to determine changes between code configs and real cloud setups.

text: Which Terraform command shows the actions that will be taken to reach the desired configuration state?

options.A: terraform plan
options.B: terraform apply
options.C: terraform validate
options.D: terraform refresh

explanation: terraform plan executes a dry run, reading actual cloud state and outlining what resources will be created, updated, or deleted.

text: What does it mean that Terraform is a 'declarative' IaC tool?

options.A: You define the desired end-state of the infrastructure, and the tool figures out how to build it
options.B: You write step-by-step scripts detailing each API command to execute
options.C: It requires declaring all variables before they can be used in configurations
options.D: The infrastructure can only be deployed in a public cloud

explanation: Declarative tools abstract the execution steps. You declare what you want, and the engine determines the dependencies and API calls.

text: What is the difference between Monitoring and Logging?

options.A: Monitoring tracks quantitative performance metrics; Logging records discrete event details
options.B: Logging is automated; Monitoring is strictly manual checking
options.C: Monitoring is only used for cloud databases; Logging is for routers
options.D: There is no difference; they are duplicate terms

explanation: Monitoring collects numerical stats (CPU, RAM, API speed) to identify health. Logging records text traces (errors, actions) to debug issues.

text: Which tool is commonly used to collect, store, and visualize metrics from target servers in real-time?

options.A: Prometheus + Grafana
options.B: Elasticsearch + Logstash
options.C: Terraform + Vault
options.D: Ansible + Jenkins

explanation: Prometheus pulls and stores time-series metrics, while Grafana overlays dashboards to visualize those metrics in real-time.

text: What does the 'ELK stack' stand for in log management?

options.A: Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana
options.B: Encryption, Logging, Key Vault
options.C: Enterprise Linux Kernel
options.D: Event Logging Kernel

explanation: ELK combines Elasticsearch (search engine), Logstash (log ingestion/clean), and Kibana (dashboard visualization) for logs.

text: Which monitoring concept refers to measuring the time it takes to service a request?

options.A: Latency
options.B: Throughput
options.C: Saturation
options.D: Availability

explanation: Latency is the round-trip time required to complete a network request or execute a compute transaction.

text: What is the role of an 'alerting threshold' in monitoring systems?

options.A: To trigger notifications automatically when a metric exceeds a safe limit (e.g. CPU > 90%)
options.B: To limit the number of logs written to disk to save space
options.C: To automatically turn off servers during weekends to save costs
options.D: To encrypt metric communication channels using TLS

explanation: Alerting rules evaluate metrics against bounds, notifying administrators (via slack, email, etc.) before outages occur.

text: What is a 'Blue-Green' deployment?

options.A: Using two identical environments, one live (blue) and one staging (green), to switch traffic instantly
options.B: Deploying the database to AWS (blue) and the web server to Azure (green)
options.C: Upgrading the operating systems of half the servers in a cluster at a time
options.D: Encrypting network connections between different geographical zones

explanation: Blue-green deployment minimizes risk and downtime by routing traffic to the idle environment once it is verified to work.

text: What is a 'Canary' deployment?

options.A: Releasing a software update to a small percentage of users before rolling it out to everyone
options.B: Deploying code updates only to developers' personal laptops for testing
options.C: Testing application security by running automated pen-test scripts
options.D: Hosting virtual machines inside on-premises datacenters

explanation: Canary deployments roll out changes incrementally to a small subset of servers or users to detect bugs early under real production load.

text: What is the benefit of using a Rolling Deployment strategy?

options.A: It updates server instances in batches, maintaining service availability without needing duplicate capacity
options.B: It rolls back the database state to the beginning of the day automatically
options.C: It compiles code files directly on the production host
options.D: It forces all users to log out before applying updates

explanation: Rolling updates replace old instances with new ones in batches, keeping some active servers alive to serve requests during updates.

text: What is a 'Rollback' in deployment pipelines?

options.A: Reverting to the previous stable software version after a new deployment fails
options.B: Deleting the git repository and cloning it again
options.C: Compiling the code into a smaller compressed file
options.D: Rebooting the database physical server host

explanation: Rollback is the recovery step of redeploying the previous working artifact or switching traffic back to the stable environment.

text: What is 'Immutable Infrastructure'?

options.A: Servers are never modified after creation; updates require deploying new server instances
options.B: Virtual machines that are locked and cannot be deleted
options.C: Databases that only support read actions without updates
options.D: Infrastructure that is hosted purely on on-premises hardware

explanation: Immutable infrastructure avoids configuration drift. You don't patch running servers; you build a new image and replace them completely.

text: What is a Microservices Architecture?

options.A: Decomposing an application into small, independent services that communicate via APIs
options.B: Building the entire website inside a single code file
options.C: Running virtual machines on micro-sized CPU capacities
options.D: Using NoSQL databases to store all application data

explanation: Microservices split monolothic apps into modular components, allowing teams to develop, test, and deploy services independently.

text: Which tool is standard for service discovery and key-value configuration in microservices clusters?

options.A: Consul
options.B: Jenkins
options.C: Docker Desktop
options.D: SonarQube

explanation: HashiCorp Consul provides service registry, health checks, and dynamic configuration keys for microservices networks.

text: What is the purpose of an API Gateway in microservices?

options.A: It acts as a single entry point, routing client requests to internal services
options.B: It compiles Python source code into machine code
options.C: It backs up database records across multiple datacenters
options.D: It restricts database connections to local connections only

explanation: API Gateways handle routing, request aggregation, authentication, and rate limiting, protecting the internal microservices network.

text: What is 'configuration drift'?

options.A: The gradual accumulation of undocumented manual changes on running servers
options.B: Moving the database files from on-premises to cloud storage
options.C: The time delay between pushing code and pipeline execution
options.D: Updating the values in the application configuration file

explanation: Drift happens when ad-hoc manual hotfixes on live servers cause their state to mismatch the definition files (IaC).

text: Which deployment model is hosted entirely on a cloud provider's shared public infrastructure?

options.A: Public Cloud
options.B: Private Cloud
options.C: On-Premises
options.D: Hybrid Cloud

explanation: Public cloud (multi-tenant) runs on resources owned and operated by third-party cloud providers, shared with other organizations.

text: In Scrum methodology, what is a 'Sprint'?

options.A: A fixed-length period (1-4 weeks) during which specific work must be completed
options.B: A daily status meeting that lasts exactly 15 minutes
options.C: A rapid code deployment to hotfix a critical production bug
options.D: The list of feature requests waiting to be prioritized

explanation: Sprints are the core heartbeat of Scrum. They are timeboxed intervals where developers complete tasks from the sprint backlog.

text: What is the purpose of the Daily Standup meeting?

options.A: To synchronize work, share progress, and identify blocking impediments
options.B: To demo the completed software product features to clients
options.C: To write code reviews for recent commits collectively
options.D: To assign new tasks to team members for the month

explanation: Daily Standups are 15-minute sync meetings where members state what they did yesterday, what they will do today, and any blockers.

text: Who is responsible for maintaining and prioritizing the Product Backlog in Scrum?

options.A: Product Owner
options.B: Scrum Master
options.C: Development Lead
options.D: System Administrator

explanation: The Product Owner represents business and customer needs, keeping the product backlog sorted and prioritized.

text: What is the role of the Scrum Master?

options.A: To facilitate Scrum processes, coach the team, and remove impediments
options.B: To write the architectural code specifications for the developers
options.C: To manage the budget and report directly to corporate executives
options.D: To test the application code for security vulnerabilities

explanation: The Scrum Master is a servant-leader who protects the team's focus, removes blockers, and ensures Scrum practices are followed.

text: What is a Sprint Retrospective?

options.A: A meeting at the end of a sprint to reflect on the process and plan improvements
options.B: A code inspection meeting to analyze recent merges
options.C: A database synchronization step run before new deployments
options.D: A test run of the application in a staging sandbox

explanation: The Retrospective focuses on continuous improvement: identifying what went well, what went wrong, and actions to improve the next sprint.

text: What Agile artifact represents a visual board showing workflow states like To Do, In Progress, and Done?

options.A: Kanban Board
options.B: Product Backlog
options.C: Sprint Burn-down chart
options.D: Gantt Chart

explanation: Kanban boards use columns and cards to represent workflow steps, visualizing tasks and managing work-in-progress (WIP).
